content: Sideburns, also referred to as side-whiskers or sideboards in the United Kingdom, are sections of facial hair that grow on the sides of a man’s face, situated in front of the ears. The term sideburns is a linguistic alteration from the original term burnsides, which was named after Ambrose Burnside. Burnside was a historical figure recognized for his distinctive facial hairstyle, which featured thick sideburns connected by a mustache while leaving the chin clean-shaven. Sideburns exhibit a wide range of variations in terms of length, shape, and style. They can be thin or wide, elaborately styled or neatly trimmed. They may be cut flat, flare outward, or taper to a point. The length of sideburns can vary, ending at mid-ear or extending further down the jawline. The term sideburns is broad and includes other specific styles of facial hair, such as Mutton Chops and Friendly Mutton Chops. Mutton Chops are named for their resemblance to the shape of a cut of mutton, extending down to the corners of the mouth. Friendly Mutton Chops, on the other hand, connect the sideburns with a mustache, creating a style similar to that worn by Ambrose Burnside himself. Sideburns can be paired with other facial hair styles, such as a mustache or goatee. However, when the hair extends from ear to ear across the chin, it is no longer classified as sideburns but rather as a beard or chin curtain. Historically, sideburns gained popularity in the early 19th century following a period in the 18th century when clean-shaven faces were the norm. This trend eventually spread to other parts of the world, including Japan. The sideburns of the 19th century were often more extravagant than those commonly seen today, resembling what we now recognize as modern-day Mutton Chops. However, like beards, sideburns fell out of fashion in the early 20th century. They experienced a resurgence in the 1960s and 1970s, particularly among younger generations. During this period, pointed sideburns became a notable symbol within the gay club scenes of San Francisco and Sydney, Australia. Due to their diverse historical associations, sideburns can be perceived as either a conservative, Victorian-era style or as a rebellious emblem of 1970s counterculture. In contemporary times, sideburns maintain a moderate level of popularity. The advent of the internet has fostered communities of enthusiasts dedicated to sideburns and beards. In certain cultural contexts, sideburns hold unique significance. For example, indigenous men in Mexico often shave their heads while allowing their sideburns to grow long, a style referred to as balcarrotas. Similarly, Colombian men are known to wear long sideburns without any accompanying facial hair. Prominent historical figures known for their distinctive sideburns include Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906), Franz Joseph I of Austria (1830–1916), Miguel Grau Seminario (1834–1879), and W. S. Gilbert (1836–1911).
